Frankly, the headline is completely inaccurate. A judge cannot "rule in favor of" a person or entity which files an amicus brief, because such briefs are by definition filed by those not party to the case. In other words, this 90% figure comes from cases in which a judge merely agreed with a gratuitous opinion offered by a company about a case to which it was wholly unrelated. Forcing them to recuse themselves on the basis of amicus briefs would allow those who file such briefs to wield undue influence over numerous cases.

To get an idea of the scope of the problems this would cause, consider that in Obergefell v. Hodges (the recent gay marriage case), 148 amicus briefs were filed. What's more, a single brief can be filed by many parties; one of those briefs was filed jointly by over 370 companies, and another was filed jointly by 300 Republican activists and holders of various public offices. Many others were filed by groups of non-profits and other interest groups. Frankly, the web of interests represented in these briefs runs so deep that by the standards of this article the entire court should have recused itself such that the case couldn't have been heard at all.

TL;DR you agree with this sort of corruption, therefore it doesn't exist.

I helped a guy and his father start a produce shop on the side of a highway in a rural area.

The first few months were great. We had people waiting on us to get there in the morning and people pulling in as we were closing. It was a sea of customers. Some even wanted to have regular orders or high dollar items (mostly local restaurants that like to keep commerce local.)

Everything was great. The three of us were able to accomplish all the tasks and the business ran smoothly.

Then, we got a meat slicer, a cold cabinet, some meats and cheeses and a bread and condiment station. All of that has to be refrigerated 24/7, which increases overhead, and required a large amount of labor. Running a small business, six days a week, with three people.. means that you're often there alone. Then, we'd have slow, old people come in and want several pounds of meat and cheese sliced and packaged, sometimes a twenty minute procedure, while produce customers stood in line. People that buy meat and cheese are also very picky and would want every slice to be a specific thickness, which isn't a problem, it just means more spent at the slicer. It was becoming obvious that the business model was flawed.

Then, we started becoming maligned. As the stress levels rose, the father and the son had frequent arguments. So, it became a two man job, which wasn't that hard, as we'd lost a chunk of customers that didn't want to wait. Having less of an emotional incentive to maintain a happy face, the son started discussing politics with customers.. which pissed off another chunk of them.. Then, he started getting short tempered, as less money was flowing in.. and his father wanted us to stay open seven days a week to make up for lost revenue.

Well, if you're in a rural area, chances are that everyone is a relative / friend / neighbor / churchmember of everyone else. For every person that had a direct reason to not come back, usually due to a dumb political argument that shouldn't have been in a place of commerce, it seemed like another handful just disappeared. Continued reduction in revenue leads to a further increase in stress, which led to us caring less.

I started to hate my job. It was almost an hour away from me, the other two guys kept wanting more and more work for less pay, customers were fewer and far in between and the likelihood that you were there, alone, from opening to close rose drastically. I also started to resent the other two guys for not working hard enough when there were there. I was the only one that would mop or clean glass or change condiment pans or sanitize equipment.. the father only came by to drop off flowers or nick knacks that he picked up at some local auction. He was grasping at straws, trying to make the business turn a profit like it first did. The son would only really pick up the produce order and help bring it into the back cooler and make sandwiches / cut meat / package produce (like clean ears of corn to put on a tray and seal.) Many things on the to-do list started to go unfinished.. and no one really cared.

Then, the son moved a woman in that he'd met on the internet two weeks prior. She was incompetent. (Truly incompetent, she didn't even know what a feminine napkin was.. she used up almost an entire roll of toilet paper every day.) But, the son moved her into his house and she get on food stamps, and the son started ringing up fake orders to launder cash from her foodstamp card into the business. He also started doing less and less work.. as in, sitting at the front register for hours at a time, letting the other work go unfinished.. and leaving early.. and moving closing time sooner, which lost our last remaining regular customers that had restaurants and could only come to the stand when their restaurant closed for the day.

Then, one day in November, they both left to go dick off and drive around right after we opened. By that point we were even serving breakfast. (Overhead, the crushing overhead.. but no one saw it or cared.) I became fed up after having to make two large, multipiece breakfast platters while other customers were coming in and it was clear that the horse was dead and we were standing around, kicking its corpse.

When they came back, I took the store keys off of my keychain and left.

It closed shortly after.

Now, it's a terrible restaurant with shit gravy that isn't even made from scratch. (I made the gravy from scratch from a recipe that I put together. I forgot to mention that. My gravy was badass.)

RIP the produce stand.. or, rather, rot in hell you inglorious, life-sucking shit-hole.

I've honestly never quit a job and felt so relieved.

I wrote software (eBooks, Children's games, Screen Savers etc.) that was sold inexpensively in specialty stores all over the USA. I had some good years and had some bad years. The final straw was the recession of 2008/2009 sales slowed considerably and by Dec of 2009 sales just stopped. I had never experienced this in the life of the business - particularly at the holiday season. Later when I was calling to collect some money owed to me I talked to one owner that had been in business for over 40 years now she couldn't even pay her heating bills. (I never got paid either but I didn't press the issue.) Literally hundreds of this type of store closed down for good. These stores were generally Mom & Pop operations and Wal-mart and the general economy had taken their toll.

I since operated another type of business that lasted about five years. I knew the demand for that item would not last forever but I had to do something. Now I have reorganized and have set up with different products that are in demand for most of the year (sadly not July / August) and I am working on a line of useful products I make myself. Things are looking up - Failure is not Final.
